newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU MAINTAINS DISTANCE FROM NATO EXPANSION PLAN.
newsitem.headline: EU MAINTAINS DISTANCE FROM NATO EXPANSION PLAN.

text.p: The European Union, preparing for the lengthy process of admitting its neighbours from eastern Europe, made clear on Tuesday it would not be dictated to by NATO, itself preparing to admit its former Cold War foes.

External Relations Commissioner Hans van den Broek, who has the task of preparing the ground for the bloc's expansion talks, told a seminar countries left out of NATO's initial expansion could not count on EU entry as a consolation prize.

"They cannot expect us to help NATO out by automatically compensating any countries that should be excluded from NATO's first wave of enlargement. No automatic compensation," he told the seminar on the link between the two projects.

Although European Commission President Jacques Santer and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana do hold informal breakfast meetings to inform each other of their respective plans, the two sides still maintain a formal distance.
U.S. Ambassador to NATO Robert Hunter stressed at the seminar the EU and NATO projects should be coordinated more as many EU members were members of the military alliance.
Van den Broek said the Commission would advise EU governments around July on how to proceed towards eastern enlargement following its own "objective criteria".

NATO, at a summit set for July 8-9 in Madrid, is expected to invite a number of eastern European hopefuls to the negotiating table, with the aim of having them on board by 1999, leaving others until later.
Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are seen as favourites for early NATO talks.

The Baltic states -- Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania -- are seen as unlikely to be in NATO's first enlargement project and feeling too close to Russia for comfort are desperately eager for strengthened links with western Europe.
NATO is currently trying to win round a deeply hostile Russia to its expansion plans, with the promise of a strengthened relationship.

Hunter told the meeting that even though all NATO applicants might not be admitted at once, the door would remain open and warned those in the first wave against trying to veto entry by their eastern neighbours later.
"If they are going to veto someone else they may as well not apply," he said, expressing a sentiment echoed by van den Broek over the EU's own plans.

Hunter said that a country could only be admitted to NATO once it could play a full role in the alliance and be a provider as well as a consumer of security on the European continent. It was not the start of talks that counted, but the finish, he said.

The fact that a country was not admitted, did not mean that NATO would not defend it if it was in its own security interest -- during the Cold War NATO would have defended non-member Sweden to protect its own interests.

Van den Broek, who refused to be drawn on the expected date of EU entry, or on the countries which might make the finishing line first, said the EU was constantly trying to help applicant countries match up to the EU's requirements.
Talks can only start once the EU has finalised inter-governmental talks on its workings to boost its structures for the day it will have 18, 20 or 25 members.
